newsitem.title: USA: Key Republican calls for new Clinton budget.
newsitem.headline: Key Republican calls for new Clinton budget.

text.p: The Republican head of the House Budget Committee called on President Bill Clinton on Monday to send Congress a new budget, saying his present one fell $69 billion short of erasing the deficit in 2002.

Rep. John Kasich of Ohio released a re-estimate of Clinton's budget by the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office. The report said the federal budget would not reach a $17 billion surplus in 2002 as Clinton proposed, making inevitable cancellation of promised tax cuts and requiring deep spending cuts if the budget were to be balanced.

"What is more astounding than that ... if we did nothing, if the president had not sent us a budget, in the next fiscal year, in 1998 the deficit would be $121 billion. But under the president's plan to balance the budget the deficit is $145 billion," Kasich said at a news conference.
"In light of these facts, the president should submit a new budget, one that is in balance in 2002," he said.
In one bright note, CBO forecast this year's deficit slightly improved at $117 billion, down from their earlier estimate of $124 billion.
Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici, Republican of New Mexico, said CBO's report confirmed his reservations about Clinton's budget.
"I hope the administration is willing to make the needed changes to achieve a real balanced budget," he said.

Office of Management and Budget spokesman Lawrence Haas disputed Kasich's criticisms. The differences were due to the age-old conflict between economic forecasts developed by administration and congressional analysts, he said.
"We feel we have fulfilled our commitment to reach balance under either OMB or CBO (economic assumptions)," Haas said.

Haas said there was no reason for Clinton to send up a new budget. "We are not sending a different document. We are fulfilling our obligation," he said, adding that the next step was the start of negotiations on the budget.
The White House has generally been more optimistic about the nation's economic future, leading to more favorable estimates for the deficit.

Based on CBO's analysis, to reach balance in 2002 most tax cuts -- including the child tax credit, education credits and retirement credits -- proposed by Clinton would have to be canceled after 2000. This would amount to a $24 billion tax increase.
In addition, CBO said an across-the-board spending cut of 4 percent would be necessary to close the gap -- almost twice as much as Clinton proposed in his alternative plan.

Kasich said that according to the congressional analysis, Clinton left 98 percent of the deficit reduction to be done after he was out of office in 2001. As scored by CBO, Clinton's plan would leave deficits of nearly $140 billion through fiscal 2000. In the next year the deficit would fall to $95 billion and to $69 billion in 2002.

CBO said Clinton's plan would produce a balanced budget in 2002 -- if tax increases and spending cuts were automatically triggered. Both of these triggers were provided in Clinton's plan but the White House maintained they would never need to be used.
Budget committee staff director Rick May said the validity of Clinton's plan was called into question because these triggers could not take place.
"They would never occur. Can you imagine Congress eliminating a tax cut in an election year? Can you imagine Congress approving across-the-board spending cuts in an election year?" May asked.
